Throughout the four-and-a-half-year war, many people have attempted to superficially declare a victor by focusing on details such as who captured where and who did what. However, war is a much more complex phenomenon that harbors ultimate strategic goals. What matters is not what territory you capture, but what that capture yields for you and at what cost. Outside observers, myself included, determine a victor or loser solely based on the dimension they are looking at, but there are ultimate goals determined by the warring parties. The final point you reach in a war is not necessarily the point where you will remain. If that were the case, the Germans would have stayed at the gates of Moscow, and the Soviets in East Berlin. In other words, nothing before, during, or after the war is static; it is dynamic.

What is important and decisive in a war is which side dictates where and how the clashing forces will fight. This initiative naturally rests largely with the side that initiates the war, that is, the side that launches the offensive with its forces. In the first phase, it dictates the battleground, and the defending side's priority is to attrit the opposing force there, strip away its advantage, and drag the war into areas of its own choosing. Although Russia started from the "right place" initially, it ignored what Ukraine was preparing for and the extent of those preparations. This is exactly what Russia lost in the Ukraine-Russia War. Russia was dragged into fighting in areas where it was forced to, rather than where it preferred to fight in Ukraine.

Ukraine's Kharkiv counter-offensive was highly critical for this reason. Moscow did not arbitrarily grant authority to Prigozhin and have him recruit men from prisons. They didn't choose to use Wagner as a battering ram simply on a whim. They knew very well that a direct advance in the Donetsk region would be agonizing and attritional. The greatest proof of this is that Wagner was brought to the brink of annihilation while merely trying to take Bakhmut, leading to Prigozhin's rebellion against Moscow. The aftermath is common knowledge... It took the Russian army exactly 26 months to reach Chasiv Yar, which is just 10 km away from Bakhmut. Back when the Russian army entered Bakhmut, I stated: "Reaching Chasiv Yar will be a long process fraught with heavy casualties."

There are many frontlines that have turned into a Bermuda Triangle for the Russian Army. Avdiivka, Kupyansk, Pokrovsk, Kurakhove, Vuhledar, and many others... These are the lines where the Russian army left behind thousands of dead, wounded, and armored vehicles for the sake of marginal advances. Then there is Kursk, which is the subject for a completely different article...

"THERE IS NO LINE OF DEFENSE, THERE IS A SURFACE OF DEFENSE"
We all know that if you are facing a force with a heavier mass than yours, rather than standing directly in front of that massive juggernaut, the most sound strategy is to redirect it and wear it down in kill zones of your own choosing. This is because high-quantity armies like the Russian army launch their offensives with high tempo and momentum; however, if countered correctly, this momentum cannot be sustained and eventually depletes. Your task is to trap this massive force coming at you across a broad front either deep within your territory or at geographic chokepoints, and grind it down in those areas.

RUSSIA'S SHIFTING OFFENSIVE TACTICS
As a result of this strategy, in 2025 and 2026, the Russian army confronted us with continuously repeated offensives in chaotic, small, and infiltration-focused groups. This was both a choice and a necessity for them, as the Russian army had largely lost its mechanized capabilities and realized that, given its current means, it did not possess an infinite pool of human resources.

This shifting approach to offensives would allow the Russian army to bypass kill zones, enable them to create localized pockets by breaching Ukrainian defenses at multiple points, and force the encircled Ukrainian troops to retreat. We must admit that the Russians successfully executed this. Exactly for this reason, it became impossible for Ukraine to trap massive forces at a single point and wear them down in deep areas, simply because such massive formations were no longer on the field. Yes, the Russian army was still suffering heavy casualties where it advanced, but its operational tempo had begun to increase.

UKRAINE'S SHIFTING DEFENSIVE TACTICS
For Ukraine, it was time for a shift in the doctrine of defense-in-depth. This had to be achieved through a doctrine that would both allow Ukraine to regain its previous advantage and force the Russian army into an even greater quagmire than before. The solution was not a narrow kill zone, but rather vast kill zones encompassing the entire frontline. This was paired with combat drones (UCAVs)—enhanced in quality and supported by sheer quantity—targeting not just military vehicles, but zeroing in on every single infantryman detected in the field like a sniper's bullet. In addition, the strategy required controlling the lines in depth using small infantry units, much like the Russian army. Furthermore, the contribution of Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) here should not be overlooked.

This is exactly what Ukraine has accomplished in 2026 and during this current month of June. Is the Russian army advancing? Of course, but this time it is slower and caught in a different kind of deadlock.

THE RUSSIAN ARMY'S CURRENT QUAGMIRE ON THE FRONTLINE
In classic offensives, if you are the attacking side, your expectations are generally clear. You endure enemy fire until you reach the designated final position, but once you arrive and entrench yourself, the immediate ordeal is over. A new logistical line is established behind you, and you resume from where you left off. This is the nature of a classic offensive.

So, what is the situation the Russian army is experiencing right now?

They attack and advance, but due to both moving in small squads and facing intense UCAV strikes, their tempo drops, and they remain continuously stuck in the kill zone. The depth of the defense is relentless. They believe they are safe when they reach their targeted final lines, but in reality, they are still standing in the kill zone. Because of this, they cannot establish secure logistical lines; logistics remain pinned down further in the rear, and their tempo plummets. As their tempo drops, they take more hits and suffer more casualties. This was one of the most critical factors that caused the Russian army's pace of occupation to hit rock bottom, so to speak, in May.

CRIPPLING LOGISTICS
If you only strike close-range frontline logistics, you will only halt the opposing force on that specific line for a short time; this is a temporary solution. If you prevent the opposing force from establishing even close-range logistics, it provides you with a massive opportunity to paralyze a much broader frontline. At that point, what you must do is strike the deep operational logistics and main supply arteries, permanently interrupting the logistical flow.

This is precisely what Ukraine has been executing in a highly concentrated manner in recent weeks. The oil depots and strategic military targets it has struck in Crimea and Krasnodar are all products of this logic. The relentless targeting of the Crimea-Melitopol and Crimea-Krasnodar logistical routes and vehicles is designed to sever this flow at its root.

The restrictions placed on gasoline sales in Russia are a direct result of Ukraine's prolonged strikes on Russia's logistical infrastructure. The fact that the Russian army has begun to suffer chronic supply issues, facing shortages even in basic necessities across all occupied territories including Crimea, stems from Ukraine intensely pounding deep operational logistics and Russia's reliance on shallow, limited logistical routes in these areas.

ADVERSARIES EDUCATE EACH OTHER
There is an important point in everything written up to here that must not be forgotten: Warring parties are each other's teachers. In other words, Russia may eventually counter the technological and operational pressure it is currently facing with similar pressure in the future. However, for Moscow to achieve its ultimate strategic goals, it must make much larger decisions. It is almost impossible to achieve this with the means currently deployed on the battlefield. It should be noted here that Ukraine is experiencing similar problems, but the cost of defense and the cost of offense are not the same. If they were, the war would have ended long ago. Ukraine is producing solutions while being acutely aware of its own reality. I cannot write more on this specific point.

DRAWING THE BOWSTRING
If you are keeping the opposing force's pace of occupation under control using autonomous systems and a small number of infantry, buying time by slowly retreating, you are trying to retain the ability to "draw the bow," or you are actively drawing that "bowstring." But what about Russia? Do you think Russia might also be drawing a bow?

If you miss the "T-point" (the critical threshold), you are no longer a proactive actor in the events, but merely a passive participant experiencing them.

desk.role: Case study — convict recruitment and death-reporting lag
desk.text: Ukraine's «Khochu Zhit» project leaked a list of 5,007 convicts recruited into the Russian army on 17 April. Mediazona verified 4,000 names and cross-checked them against the Probate Registry four times over five months: 118 dead on 26 April, 198 on 20 May, 352 a month later, 807 on 10 September — one in five. 84.5% of the deaths occurred between January and March (81 in January, 316 in February, 285 in March); only 125 between May and August. Only 112 of these 807 people (one in seven) appear in the open-source database.
desk.caveat: This is a case study based on a single list; it cannot be generalized to all Russian losses. But it shows that public death information lags even behind the official record.

desk.caveat: The source's own caveat: the date is not certain ("probably June, definitely before 6 July"); there is no high-resolution imagery evidence, Copernicus only gives a hint.

desk.role: Institute for the Study of War — monthly advance assessment
desk.text: July 2026 in review: Russian forces advanced only 37.85 km² for the month — an area smaller than Manhattan, averaging 1.22 km² a day. Including infiltration operations, 121.56 km². For comparison, the figure was 455.74 km² in July 2025. That same month Ukraine's General Staff reported 42,860 Russian losses — by ISW's count, the highest monthly level of the war. That works out to an average of 1,132 losses for every km² captured or infiltrated.

desk.role: Institute for the Study of War
desk.text: Russia launched 376 missiles at Ukraine in July — the highest monthly total since large-scale strikes began (the previous peak was 288, in February). Assessed to be relying increasingly on the S-400 and Zircon to make up for a shortfall in ballistic missile production.

desk.role: Institute for the Study of War
desk.text: A large-scale air-defense suppression operation in Krasnodar Krai overnight targeted a Tor-M2 system and Nebo-S, Gamma-S1M, Nebo-U, Kasta-2E2 and 37T radars. The strikes on Shabelskoye and Kamyshevatskaya were confirmed with geolocated footage. Russia has also begun using new jet-powered Banderol and Geran-4 «Seeker» drones against Black Sea ports and railways.

Russia gained a net +36 km² in July (which could rise to as much as 88 km² with delayed confirmations); the team revised the May–July figure down by 52 km². Official confirmation is pending for two Ukrainian advances (≥49 and ≥83 km²). DeepState's assessment is clear: Russia's goal of capturing the entire Donetsk oblast in 2026 is not realistic — at the current pace it has no chance even by 2027.

desk.role: FT investigation, in cooperation with Frontelligence Insight and Sapienza University
desk.text: A night-light analysis of 29 refineries by Sapienza University's Fabio Sabatini: Ukraine's campaign has knocked out more than 30% of Russia's operating refining capacity, 45% of its nominal capacity. The result is Russia's most severe fuel crisis since the collapse of the Soviet Union. The damage is still visible from satellites months later.

desk.role: Frontelligence Insight — founder, former Ukrainian officer
desk.text: Special report, «Ukraine's Military Leadership Change»: 43-year-old Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi replaced Syrskyi as Ukraine's youngest-ever chief of the General Staff. The team's warning is measured — mobilization reform will take 6-12 months to show results, and no single commander-in-chief can overcome the structural constraints imposed by manpower, resources and a war that keeps dragging on.

An assessment that Ukraine's General Staff estimates of Russian losses are "not far from reality" for 2026: Russia's internal reporting shows roughly 1,000 losses a day, more than half of them deaths.

Announced that strikes at 500–2,000 km depth rose 1,150% in 2026. In June alone, 2,359 deep-strike missions were flown, damaging 172 military-industrial and energy facilities. During the «Crimean Switch Off» phase from 1 July to 2 August, 177 energy targets were hit in the south; 13 more nodes in Crimea in the last 72 hours.

desk.role: Joint named-casualty list project with the BBC's Russian service
desk.text: The confirmed Russian death toll reached 248,800 (+2,867 since mid-July). Breakdown: more than 86,600 volunteers, 26,200 recruited from prison, 19,600 mobilized, 7,465 officers. Date of death is known in 218,400 cases — about 93% of confirmed losses. This list is a lower bound; the statistical estimate (Probate Registry, end of 2025) is ~352,000.

Latest assessment: despite Gerasimov's 3 July claim that Kostyantynivka had been fully captured, Russia controls only half of the city. Separately, reported that the Black Sea Fleet has begun fitting anti-drone cages to its Kilo-class submarines, and that the main Navy Day parade was cancelled on security grounds.

desk.role: Unnamed Russian military blogger accounts — ISW compilation
desk.text: Pro-Kremlin bloggers claimed advances near Torske, west of Kostyantynivka, and southeast of Dobropillia (Matiyashevo). The same bloggers complained for a second month running that Ukraine's long-range strikes were not letting up, and criticized officials for blaming the damage on "falling debris" instead of acknowledging successful Ukrainian attacks.
desk.caveat: An unverified partisan claim — ISW has not confirmed these advance claims with geolocated footage.
